newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/Investors roll out to Jan 1998.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/Investors roll out to Jan 1998.

text.p: Some investors in large cap blue chip options appeared to be rolling January call positions out to January 1998.
Select January 1998 calls on shares of Johnson & Johnson, Coca-Cola Co and Intel Corp each traded on heavy volume, as did select January 1997 calls.

"As we get close to expiration, there is a lot of volume in January options in big names with LEAPS (long term equity anticipation securities) attached," said Michael Schwartz, managing director at Oppenheimer & Co.
In Johnson & Johnson, the January 1998 40 call traded 8,465 contracts. The option had open interest through Wednesday of 611 contracts.
The Johnson & Johnson January 30 call, which expires at the end of next week, traded 5,863 contracts.
"Somebody must be rolling over," Schwartz said, noting that the January 30 call, with open interest of 9,248 through Wednesday, had the largest open interest of any Johnson & Johnson option.
Johnson & Johnson shares finished 3/8 higher at 51-1/2.
In similar fashion, the Coca-Cola January 1998 30 call traded 5,465 contracts. Its open interest was 4,490.
The January 30 call traded 5,426 contracts. Its open interest was nearly 21,000 contracts.

Other busy Coca-Cola options included the January 45 call, with volume of about 2,400, the January 45 put, with volume of 2,100, the February 45 put, with volume of about 1,100, and the February 55 call, with volume of 1,125.
Coca-Cola shares ended at 53-7/8, up 1/2.
Schwartz said the LEAP volume in Intel was a bit curious as it was in a deep in-the-money call.
The Intel January 1998 65 call traded 5,295 contracts in one block at 80-1/2. Open interest was 513.
Intel shares rose 3/4 to 143.
Several January calls were active, led by the 140, which traded 3,287 contracts, and the 145, which traded 3,170.
Schwartz said the Intel LEAPS volume was curious as it appeared to be an opening position because the open interest through Wednesday was only 513 contracts.
"Unless there's some tax motivation, it doesn't make sense to buy those because you can buy the stock on margin for less than 80-1/2," he said.
Schwartz said if the investor expected some "horrific" news, a cheaper strategy would be to sell the stock short and buy puts.
